960.title: Tagore's Gitanjali (public domain, 1912)
960.hook: a small reed flute, carried over hills, played by someone else's breath
960.howItsDone: Tagore wrote the Gitanjali songs in Bengali, and in Bengal his songs are still sung at home, in schools and at gatherings; readers elsewhere often know the poems through his own English prose versions.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Gandhi's Gita with the person of steady wisdom: the tortoise drawing in, the sea staying level while the rivers pour in.

A reed flute is a plain thing. A hollow stalk, a few holes, nothing inside. It makes no sound on its own. Somebody has to carry it and breathe through it, and then a song comes out that the reed could never have made by itself. A poet opened a book with that picture. The English edition of his songs carries a short subtitle, Song Offerings, and says it was translated by the author from the original Bengali. The poet is Rabindranath Tagore. The book is Gitanjali.
screen: `A REED FLUTE MAKES NO SOUND ALONE.` → `SONG OFFERINGS.` → `TAGORE'S GITANJALI.`

segments.voice: Here is how the first poem opens, in Tagore's own English: "Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure. This frail vessel thou emptiest again and again, and fillest it ever with fresh life." The speaker doesn't fill himself. He's emptied, and filled, by someone he addresses only as thou. Then the flute arrives. This little reed, the poem says, has been carried over hills and dales, and thou has breathed through it melodies always new. So the singer, in his own picture, is the instrument and not the musician. That turns the title around. A song offering sounds like something a person makes and hands up to God. But here the songs were breathed in from the other side first. What gets offered back is what was given. The poem ends on hands: the infinite gifts come only on these very small hands, and ages pass, and still thou pourest, and still there is room to fill. Among the modern teachers, this poem keeps company with old things. A singer pouring out songs to a divine thou is close to the bhakti poets, who sang to God as a lover or a friend. And the vessel emptied and refilled sits near the Gita teaching we just spent days on: the work done, the fruit let go, and something flowing through. Tagore doesn't name a god in this poem, and doesn't argue. He says thou, and keeps listening. Some readers hear Krishna in it, some the one Self of the Upanishads, some simply a person grateful to be alive.

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up: small hands. Breathe out fully, as if the vessel is being emptied, then let the next breath come in on its own, and notice that you didn't make it; it arrived. If you pray, you can hold the breath that comes in as the gift the poem talks about; if not, just notice that there's still room for one more.

961.title: Tagore's Gitanjali (public domain, 1912)
961.hook: a poet tells a worshiper to open the temple doors and look outside
961.howItsDone: Hindus pray in many ways, with beads and chanting in a temple corner as well as through daily work, and Tagore's poem is one poet's voice within the tradition, often read as a call to find God among working people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tagore's Gitanjali opened at its first poem: the frail vessel emptied and filled, the little reed flute, and still room to fill.

A dark corner of a temple. The doors are shut. Someone sits there with a string of beads, chanting, eyes closed. It's a real and honored form of devotion. And in one Gitanjali poem, the poet walks up to that person and says, in effect: stop. Open your eyes. Your God isn't before you. Today, poem eleven, and where Tagore says to look instead.
screen: `A DARK CORNER, DOORS SHUT.` → `OPEN YOUR EYES.` → `WHERE TO LOOK INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Here are the opening lines, in Tagore's own English: "Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee!" Then he says where God is: "He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones." God is with them in sun and in shower, the poem says, his garment covered in dust, and it tells the worshiper to put off the holy mantle and come down onto the dusty soil too. The poem doesn't sneer at the worshiper. But it does say plainly: leave the beads, and later, the flowers and incense too. Its sharpest picture is the shut doors: a devotion walled off from people working in the sun misses where God already is. Tagore's family belonged to the Brahmo Samaj, a reform movement wary of image worship, and the poem carries that voice. Hindus who pray with beads and flowers may answer that their worship is where they learn to see God in the field. The worshiper hopes for deliverance, freedom from all this. Where is such deliverance to be found, the poem asks, since the master himself has joyfully taken on the bonds of creation? God isn't escaping the world. God is bound up in it, on purpose, gladly. The poem closes by telling the worshiper to meet him and stand by him in toil and in the sweat of the brow. The place of worship and the place of work turn out to be the same place.
screen: `LEAVE THE CHANTING, OPEN YOUR EYES.` · `GOD IS WITH THE TILLER AND THE PATHMAKER.` · `THE COMPLAINT IS THE SHUT DOOR.` · `GOD HAS TAKEN ON THE BONDS OF CREATION.` · then, large: `MEET HIM IN TOIL.`

segments.voice: Open your eyes and let your gaze rest on what's in front of you. Bring to mind someone whose work you depend on and rarely see, whoever grew today's food, laid the road outside or cleans the building, and stay with one of them, at work in sun or rain. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, right where they're working; if not, simply keep them in view, with some gratitude.

962.title: Tagore's Gitanjali (public domain, 1912)
962.hook: a prayer that is one long sentence, made of the word where
962.tomorrow: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
962.howItsDone: Poem 35 of Gitanjali, 'Where the mind is without fear', is one of the poems some readers learn by heart and recite, at school or at gatherings about freedom and education.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Tagore's Gitanjali, the temple doors came open: God with the tiller and the pathmaker, garment covered in dust.

Where. It's a small word, usually a question. Where are my keys? Where did the afternoon go? In one Gitanjali poem, Tagore takes that word and stacks it, line on line, where, where, where, like someone describing a place they long to live in. Only at the very end does the sentence land, and the whole thing turns out to be a prayer. Today, poem thirty-five, our last day with Tagore.
screen: `WHERE. A SMALL WORD.` → `LINE ON LINE: WHERE, WHERE, WHERE.` → `THE SENTENCE LANDS AS A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: It begins, in Tagore's own English: "Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; Where knowledge is free; Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls." A place where words come from the depth of truth. Where tireless striving reaches toward perfection. Where the clear stream of reason hasn't lost its way in the dry desert sand of dead habit. These are conditions of mind and spirit, not buildings or borders: fear, a head held up or bowed down, walls that split people into fragments, habit that dries reason out. Then the last line turns the whole sentence toward someone: "Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake." My Father. The poem was addressed all along, like the first poem with its thou. It isn't a speech about a nation. It's a request, made to God, that a people wake into a certain kind of freedom. Readers hear it more than one way: about a country and its future, or about any single person waking from fear and habit. The poem lets both stand. One more line points at where this path goes next. Just before the end, it asks for a place where the mind is led forward by thee into ever-widening thought and action. Thought and action, led forward by God. Over three days, Tagore has given us a flute breathed through, a God found in the dust of work, and a mind waking into freedom. Next, we go back to the Gita, slowly, to the chapters about action itself.
screen: `WHERE THE MIND IS WITHOUT FEAR.` · `STATES OF MIND, NOT BORDERS.` · `MY FATHER, LET MY COUNTRY AWAKE.` · `LED FORWARD INTO THOUGHT AND ACTION.` · then, large: `INTO THAT HEAVEN OF FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Lift the head a little, chin level and neck long: the head held high, without strain. Then go through the poem's wheres one at a time and ask each gently of yourself, where is there fear in me, where is a narrow wall, where has a habit gone dry, without fixing anything. If you pray, you can end with the poem's own last line: into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake.

963.title: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
963.hook: Arjuna catches his teacher in what looks like a contradiction
963.tomorrow: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
963.howItsDone: Some Hindus begin a day's work, or a meal, by mentally offering it to God, and some Gita study groups read chapter three alongside a classical commentary such as Shankara's.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Tagore's Gitanjali with a prayer made of wheres, and a mind led forward into thought and action.

If understanding is better than action, why push me into this terrible deed? That, in paraphrase, is how chapter three of the Gita begins. In chapter two, Krishna praised a steady understanding and said plain action falls far below it. And all along, he'd been telling Arjuna to stand up and fight. Arjuna is confused, and a little irritated. Your words seem mixed, he says. Tell me the one thing that's good for me. Now we read these chapters again, slowly, with the old commentators at our elbow.
screen: `WHY PUSH ME INTO THIS DEED?` → `YOUR WORDS SEEM MIXED.` → `READ AGAIN, WITH COMMENTARY.`

segments.voice: Krishna's first answer is almost blunt. Nobody can stay even a moment without acting. Every being is made to act by the forces of its own nature. Sitting still is an act. Breathing is an act. Even keeping the body alive, he says a few verses later, couldn't happen without action. So the question was never whether to act, but how. Here Krishna brings in an old word: yajna, sacrifice, offering. The world is bound by action, he says, except action done as offering. Do your work in that spirit, free of clinging. Then a short creation story. In the beginning, the Creator brought forth beings together with sacrifice and said: by this you will flourish. You nourish the gods, and the gods will nourish you. Rain, food, work, offering, rain again. Krishna calls it a wheel set turning, and says a person who takes from it and doesn't help turn it lives in vain. So karma, in chapter three, is first the plain word for action, and only then the web of consequences it sets going. Action you can't avoid, done as an offering, keeps the wheel turning instead of binding you to it. Shankara, glossing sacrifice in this verse, says it means the Lord himself, and quotes an older Vedic line: sacrifice is Vishnu. So for him, action done as offering is action done for God. Other readers keep the word closer to the ritual fire and the shared work of a household. Either way, the verse says the same thing about the doer: act, and let go of the grip.
screen: `NOBODY STAYS A MOMENT WITHOUT ACTING.` · `THE QUESTION IS WHAT KIND OF ACTION.` · `ACTION DONE AS OFFERING DOESN'T BIND.` · `THE WHEEL: NOURISH AND BE NOURISHED.` · then, large: `HELP THE WHEEL TURN.`

segments.voice: For the first few breaths, try to do nothing at all, and notice that you can't: the breath goes on, the heart goes on, the body keeps its balance. Then find one place in an ordinary day where you mostly take from the wheel and give little back, without judging it, and one small way to put something back. If you pray, you can hold that small return before Krishna, or the one you pray to.
Karma. In chapter three, first the plain word for action, which nobody escapes, and action done as offering, which keeps the wheel turning.

964.title: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
964.hook: a king who reached the highest goal without leaving the palace
964.tomorrow: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
964.howItsDone: Some Hindus who study the Gita point to King Janaka as the model of a person who lives in the world and knows the Self, and some study circles dwell on the verse on one's own dharma (3.35).

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma in chapter three: nobody stays a moment without acting, and action done as offering keeps the wheel turning.

Janaka was a king. He had a palace, a court, a kingdom to run: taxes, quarrels, harvests. And the Hindu tradition remembers him as a sage, someone who knew the Self while sitting on a throne. Halfway through chapter three, Krishna reaches for his name. Janaka and others like him, he says, reached perfection through action itself. Not by walking away. By doing the work. It opens the second half of the chapter, and a word that holds the whole world together.
screen: `JANAKA: A KING AND A SAGE.` → `PERFECTION THROUGH ACTION.` → `A WORD THAT HOLDS THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: The word is lokasangraha. Loka is the world, the people in it. Sangraha is a holding together, a gathering. Krishna tells Arjuna to act with that in view. Then he gives a very human reason. Whatever a leading person does, others do too. Whatever standard they set, the world follows. So the way you work isn't private. Somebody is watching. Then Krishna points at himself. There's nothing in the three worlds, he says, that I have to do, nothing I lack, nothing to gain. And yet I keep acting. If I stopped, people everywhere would follow my path, and the worlds would fall apart. So the wise should act without attachment, as the unwise act with it, for the sake of holding the world together. And they shouldn't unsettle the minds of people attached to their work; let them keep working, and show them how by example. A few verses later: better one's own dharma, even done imperfectly, than another's done well. Your own place in the holding-together, even if it's clumsy. Commentators weigh this differently. Shankara, who holds that liberation finally comes through knowledge, reads the call to act here as fitting for those still on the way, and as an example for others. Some modern readers took lokasangraha as close to the heart of the whole Gita. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, in his long commentary called the Gita Rahasya, read it that way, as a charge to keep working for the world's welfare. The verses can carry both. Either way, karma here isn't only my action. It's one thread in a cloth that a lot of other people are wearing.
screen: `LOKASANGRAHA: HOLDING THE WORLD TOGETHER.` · `WHAT A LEADER DOES, OTHERS FOLLOW.` · `KRISHNA NEEDS NOTHING, AND STILL ACTS.` · `BETTER YOUR OWN DHARMA, IMPERFECT.` · then, large: `ONE THREAD IN THE CLOTH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people who see how you work, a child, a coworker, a younger sibling, a neighbor, and just notice that they're there. Then take one thing you do every day, the dishes, a meeting, a commute, and ask what it teaches without a word, seeing it as one thread in the cloth. If you pray, you can offer that one thread.
Karma. Action done for lokasangraha, the holding together of the world, the way King Janaka did it, and the way Krishna says he does.

965.howItsDone: In Hindu teaching lineages, a teaching is received from a teacher in an unbroken parampara, and Gita 4.7–8, 'whenever dharma declines', is a verse some Hindus learn by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma as lokasangraha: King Janaka reaching perfection through action, and work done to hold the world together.

The sun. Manu. Ikshvaku. Three names at the start of chapter four, and they're a chain. Krishna says he taught this yoga, the yoga of action, to Vivasvan, the sun. Vivasvan told it to Manu. Manu told it to his son Ikshvaku. And so it was handed on, from one royal sage to the next. Then, over a long stretch of time, Krishna says, it was lost. That's why he's telling it again, now, to Arjuna, on a battlefield.
screen: `THE SUN, MANU, IKSHVAKU.` → `HANDED ON, KING TO KING.` → `LOST, AND TOLD AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The Gita's word for this handing on is parampara: one after another, teacher to student. And Krishna tells Arjuna why it's coming to him: because you are my devotee and my friend, and this is a deep secret. Arjuna, being Arjuna, hears a problem. Your birth was recent, he says. The sun's was long ago. How could you have taught him? Krishna's answer is the turn of the chapter. Many births have passed, for me and for you. I know them all. You don't. Then he describes his own coming. Though unborn, and Lord of all beings, he comes into being through his own power, his own maya. And he says when: whenever dharma declines and its opposite rises, he sends himself forth, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back on its feet. Here's the link to our word. In the next verse, Krishna calls his birth and his action, his karma, divine. Whoever truly knows them isn't born again on leaving the body, but comes to him. So the one teaching the yoga of action is also acting: taking birth, entering the world, doing the work. The commentators read his coming differently. Shankara speaks of the Lord appearing to take a body by his own maya, while remaining unborn. Ramanuja insists the Lord's births are real, taken freely by his own will, not forced on him by karma, as ours are. Both read the same verse. And the chapter's shape holds either way: the teaching of action comes down a chain of people, and it's renewed by one who acts.
screen: `PARAMPARA: ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` · `MANY BIRTHS: I KNOW THEM, YOU DON'T.` · `WHENEVER DHARMA DECLINES, I COME.` · `HIS BIRTH AND KARMA ARE DIVINE.` · then, large: `RENEWED BY ONE WHO ACTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing someone taught you, a recipe, a prayer, a knot, how to apologize, and picture the person who taught you, then, if you can, the person who taught them. Let the chain run back as far as you can see, into people you'll never know, and sit with the whole line behind one small skill. If you pray, you can give thanks for the whole chain.
Karma. In chapter four, a yoga of action handed down teacher to student, lost, and told again by one whose own birth and action are divine.
Your line: a teaching lost and told again. Tomorrow, a verse some families say before eating. Until then.

966.title: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
966.hook: a verse said over a plate of food, where everything in the meal is Brahman
966.carry: the offering, the fire and the one who offers
966.tomorrow: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
966.howItsDone: Some Hindu families and schools recite Gita 4.24, 'brahmarpanam brahma havir', as a grace before meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma handed down: the sun, Manu, Ikshvaku, a teaching lost and told again by one whose birth and action are divine.

Before the first bite, in some Hindu homes, someone says a line in Sanskrit over the plate. Brahmarpanam brahma havir. It's from chapter four of the Gita, an odd thing to say before dinner: it's a verse about a fire sacrifice. The offering is Brahman. The thing offered is Brahman. It's poured into the fire, which is Brahman, by the one offering, who is Brahman. A meal, a fire, a giver, all one.
screen: `A LINE SAID OVER THE PLATE.` → `THE OFFERING IS BRAHMAN.` → `ONE ACT, SEEN ALL THE WAY THROUGH.`

segments.voice: A few verses earlier, Krishna sets a puzzle. What is action, and what is inaction? Even the wise are confused about this. His answer: the one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among people, and does all their work in yoga. Shankara reads this as seeing that the Self never acts, even while the body is busy. Ramanuja reads it as seeing knowledge of the self alive inside work done without attachment. Then Krishna describes such a person. Their acts have been burned in the fire of knowledge. They've let go of clinging to the fruit; they're always content, depending on nothing, and though they keep acting, they do nothing at all. Then the meal verse: Brahman is the offering, Brahman the oblation, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman. The one who sees Brahman in the act goes to Brahman. Our word has traveled since chapter three began: action you can't avoid, done as offering; action for the world, the way Janaka did it; action handed down through teachers and taken up by God; and now action seen so clearly that the doer, the deed and the fire are one thing. Later in the chapter Krishna says it plainly: as a kindled fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns all actions to ash. Look back over the week: Tagore's flute, God in the dust, a mind waking. And the Gita's long answer to Arjuna's complaint: you can't stop acting, so learn to see what acting is.
screen: `INACTION IN ACTION, ACTION IN INACTION.` · `ACTS BURNED IN THE FIRE OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `BRAHMAN OFFERS BRAHMAN INTO BRAHMAN.` · `THE WEEK: FLUTE, DUST, WHEEL, FIRE.` · then, large: `SEE THE ACT ALL THE WAY THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the last thing you ate, or the next, and go through it the way the verse does: the food, the hands that lift it, the hunger it goes into, the one who's eating, each part slowly, then all of them together as one act. If you pray, you can say the verse's opening words, brahmarpanam brahma havir, or a grace from your own tradition; if not, simply rest in the whole act at once.
Karma. In chapter four, action seen so clearly that the offering, the fire and the one who offers are one, and the act itself turns to ash in the fire of knowledge.
